items_missed: Never asked 'how are you today?' — the customer asked her instead ('It is. How are you? That was quick?') and Joanna answered around it without returning the question.

Availability was never confirmed. She recapped the requested date — 'right now you're planning to do this move on the 14th of October which is a Wednesday, is that right?' — but never said Einstein has that day open. On a call where she later asks for the booking, never establishing that the date is available leaves the ask standing on nothing.

The 'pricing is super simple' opener was not used. 'I'll just of course explain to you our pricing and how you work as well' is a transition, not the framing line, and 'what's good about our pricing, it's all inclusive rates' arrives after the rate rather than in front of it.

Estimate padded above her own stated range. She said 'typically a three bedroom apartment of this size usually can take five to seven hours to complete' and then quoted 'the seven and a half to eight and a half hour mark' — a full hour and a half past her own top end — and then budgeted at the highest number in that range ($1,615 at 8.5 hours). See the estimate-accuracy flag in the coaching note; the fourth-floor elevator justifies going to the top of five-to-seven, not past it.

The quote was built on the wrong home profile and she said so. 'I'll just quote you for like a typical three bedroom apartment' — but the customer had already corrected her: 'it's a two bedroom with a study.' She acknowledged the correction ('I see. Okay, no problem') and then priced the larger profile anyway.

Drive time and trip fee never addressed. Both addresses were on file and the drive between them was never mentioned as a time factor or a fee factor, so the customer does not know whether her $1,615 includes the drive.
Traffic never mentioned as a variable on a mid-week daytime move across Houston.

Save Your Ass was half-delivered and never turned into instructions. She landed the core idea twice — 'the shorter to move the lower the cost at the end of the day' and 'the shorter it will be the lower the cost' — but she never told the customer how to make it shorter. No consolidation examples (loose items in drawers, closet odds and ends, photos off the walls), no 'take a carload,' and no sense-check close. This was the best Save-Your-Ass setup in the entire batch: the customer gets keys on September 30 and does not move until October 14, meaning she has two full weeks of access to both places, and she described her own plan out loud — 'as soon as we get the keys and this is how we moved into ours now, so when the movers come, we're already unpacked and they're moving our big stuff and we're done.' Joanna affirmed the plan but never coached it, never quantified it, and never turned it into hours off the clock.

No BOLDED-details framing on the email and no 'reply with any corrections' ask. She invited a follow-up send ('feel free to send us a photos or inventory list of everything we're moving for you, we'll just review it accordingly') but that is about scope, not about verifying what is in the confirmation email — so the email_handoff differentiator does not count.
No 'any other questions before I let you go?' — the customer closed the call herself ('Perfect, thank you so much. I really appreciate all your help').
Hours and how to reach us never given.

No Worries Damage Coverage was named correctly but under-explained. 'A no worries damage coverage of $2,000 for any accidental damages' landed the brand and the number but not 'repair, replace, or reimburse' and not the 60-cents-per-pound industry baseline that makes $2,000 sound like a lot instead of a little.

Clarity cost her twice. The customer had to ask her to repeat the total — 'I'm sorry. I what was the total. It, it's loud here. I didn't hear you' — and the rate came out as a stumble ('It's $9,595 per hour. Per mover'). On a call where the whole deliverable is two numbers, both numbers required a second pass.
'Okay, no problem' and 'yes ma'am' are used well past the point of meaning anything — roughly two dozen times between them. The warmth is real but the vocabulary carrying it never varies.
top_strength: This is the most complete discovery-and-differentiator call in the batch and it is not close. The probe section is a clean 9 out of 9 — she got both addresses, corrected the home size against the customer's own words, established the fourth floor and the elevator, asked about extra rooms and storage units, asked about packing services explicitly ('Are you planning to do all the packing yourself or do you need help with packing as well?'), negotiated a working box number when the customer did not have one, asked about specialty items by weight ('anything that you think is over 300 or 500 pounds like a safe piano kind of weight'), and then did something almost nobody does: she measured the walk in two segments. First 'the walking business from where we can park to the elevator at the first floor... about thirty to forty feet, do you think it's just within that range?', then, after the customer said her door is 'at the very end of the hallway,' she followed up on the fourth-floor leg separately using the school-bus equivalent from the rubric. That is the walk-distance bullet executed the way it is meant to be executed. Her differentiator block is the strongest of the week — three of five hit explicitly and in sequence: Meet Your Mover delivered with the reasoning attached ('rest assured we don't take daily contract. The workers, our guys are the most experienced movers in the industry and we'll send you their names ahead of time to let you know who's coming to help out with the move'), On-Time Guarantee stated with the discount mechanism intact ('if we run late on the time we schedule, we provide discounts by the end of the day'), and the no-hidden-fees list itemized ('no credit card fees, no travel fees, no transportation fees'). Her clock explanation is a perfect 4 of 4 and the only one in the batch that is: start trigger, minimum, fifteen-minute increments, and a real sense-check — 'We only start the time once we arrive at the pickup location and open the contract, you can have us for as long as you need us. Now for any move, there's just a two and a half hour minimum, once we go over that, we only charge in fifteen minute increments. Does that make sense?' She also asked for the booking properly and paired it with the no-deposit differentiator in one breath: 'We actually do not take any deposits. I can definitely get you on the schedule right now, there's no risk in securing a spot. If you need to make changes later, all you have to do is give us a call.' And she opened by accommodating the customer's constraint instead of steamrolling it — told 'I'm at work for another half hour,' she offered 'I can actually send everything in the email too if that's better for you.'
coaching_note: Estimate-accuracy flag, and this one goes straight into the bottom-4 file. Joanna stated the typical range for this home size herself — five to seven hours — and then quoted seven and a half to eight and a half, budgeting the customer at the very top ($1,615). The stated justification was the fourth floor and the walk, which is a legitimate reason to price at seven, the top of her own range. It is not a reason to price a full hour and a half past it, and there are three facts on this call pushing the other way: the home is 1,250 square feet, it is actually a two-bedroom with a study rather than the three-bedroom profile she priced, and the customer is moving every box and every storage unit herself with two weeks of overlapping access — 'there's not gonna be boxes, it's gonna be literally like our furniture.' Joanna is quoting a full three-bedroom apartment's worth of time for a furniture-only job. This is the padding pattern, and it is worth noting that it shows up here on an apartment, which is the side of the book where the known bias usually runs the other way — the underlying instinct is not really about home type, it is about wanting the number to be safe. When this job books, pull the actual against 8.5 hours; it is a clean test. The coaching line is specific: when the customer tells you they are moving the boxes themselves, that comes off the estimate, it does not get absorbed into the buffer. Highest-leverage fix for the sale itself: she asked for the booking once, got a soft 'obviously I'm not finalizing anything today, today's the first day I'm getting all the information,' and did not come back to it. That is a shopping objection, not a no, and the answer she already had in her pocket was the one she had used sixty seconds earlier — no deposit, no risk. 'Totally understood, Robin. Since there's no deposit and no cancellation fee, let me pencil in Wednesday the 14th so it's held while you compare. If you find something better, one phone call and it's gone — but October dates go fast and it costs you nothing to hold it.' A soft hold on a no-deposit booking is not pressure, and it is the difference between a lead and a job. Second priority: Save Your Ass, which is the biggest single point loss on an otherwise excellent call. The customer handed her the setup — keys on September 30, move on October 14, two weeks of access to both places, and a stated plan to pre-move everything herself. Joanna said 'the shorter the move the lower the cost' and stopped. What that moment needed: 'Since you've got the keys two weeks early, that's genuinely money in your pocket. Anything small and awkward — what's loose in the drawers, the closet odds and ends, the art off the walls, the bird cage — take a carload over each time you go. Every trip like that comes straight off your clock on the 14th. And if you can get the storage units emptied into the apartment before we come, the guys never leave the building. Does that make sense?' That advice is also the honest fix for the padded estimate — it would have let her quote six and a half hours with confidence instead of eight and a half with a buffer. Third, and this is the one to pair with the CET clarity work: the customer could not hear the total the first time and the rate came out garbled. On every quoting call, the rate and the total should be said slowly, once, in a short sentence of their own, and then repeated back — 'So that's one hundred ninety dollars an hour for two movers. At eight hours, sixteen hundred and fifteen dollars total. I'll have both of those in the email.' Two numbers are the only thing the customer has to remember; everything else can be fast.
phone_presence_notes: Genuinely patient and customer-first — she offered to switch the whole conversation to email when the customer said she was at work, met the 'this is the last move I'm doing' venting with real recognition ('I know, I understand'), and the customer closed with 'I really appreciate all your help. You have an awesome evening'; capped at 4 because the warmth runs on a very narrow vocabulary ('okay, no problem' and 'yes ma'am' roughly two dozen times) and because the customer had to ask her to repeat the one number that mattered.
audio_review_reason: Clarity is the open question on this call and the transcript cannot settle it. The customer explicitly said she could not hear the total ('it's loud here. I didn't hear you'), and the three most important figures all transcribe as garbled — the rate as 'It's $9,595 per hour. Per mover,' the walk equivalent as 'do you think it's about $30, I mean, do you think it's about 23 school buses,' and the minimum as 'we start by the twenty and a half hour.' Whether these are transcription artifacts or actual delivery stumbles determines whether the coaching here is about pace and enunciation or nothing at all, and this rep sits in the CET group where that distinction is being actively worked.
